statement: As summarized in the US Surgeon General's reports of 2006 and 2014 (narrative reviews that grade their conclusions; the figures are second-hand here, and the 2014 report builds on the 2006 one, so the two are not independent replication), people who do not smoke but breathe other people's tobacco smoke, compared with people who are not exposed, are linked to illness in the authors' graded judgments. In children (2006): sufficient to infer a causal relationship for sudden infant death syndrome, lower respiratory illness in infancy and early childhood (greatest from the mother's smoking), middle ear disease, cough, phlegm, wheeze and breathlessness and ever having asthma at school age, onset of wheeze illnesses in early childhood, lower lung function in childhood, and a small reduction in birth weight; suggestive but not sufficient for preterm delivery, onset of childhood asthma and several childhood cancers; inadequate to infer the presence or absence of a causal relationship for fertility, spontaneous abortion, congenital malformations, and children's thinking and behaviour. In adults: sufficient for lung cancer in people who never smoked (pooled studies indicate a 20 to 30 percent higher risk from living with a person who smokes) and for coronary heart disease (pooled relative risks indicate a 25 to 30 percent higher risk), and for odour annoyance and nasal irritation; stroke was graded suggestive in 2006 and sufficient in 2014 (an increase of about 20 to 30%); several respiratory symptoms, adult-onset asthma, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and breast cancer were graded suggestive, and others inadequate. The 2014 report adds that smokefree laws were followed by fewer coronary events in people under 65 (sufficient). The parts read give no relative or absolute risks for the children's outcomes or for adult outcomes other than lung cancer, coronary heart disease and stroke. The 2006 report states that there is no risk-free level of exposure to secondhand smoke; its chapter 1 gives no separate derivation or threshold analysis for the statement. By the editors' reading, the nearest reasoning in the part read is toxicological and mechanistic (more than 50 carcinogens in secondhand smoke; raised urinary levels of a tobacco-specific carcinogen's metabolites in people who do not smoke; a clot-promoting effect, harm to the lining of blood vessels and atherosclerosis in animals) together with the raised risks above and the report's statement that adults have immediate adverse effects on the cardiovascular system, while the report adds that the cancer risk is lower than from active smoking because the carcinogen dose is substantially lower and that, from what is known of dose and mechanisms, it anticipates only slightly or modestly raised risks for some associations, such as lung cancer. The report says exposure misclassification and near-universal background exposure may bias estimates toward no effect, that lifestyle differences may bias them the other way, and that uncertainty around pooled estimates may exceed what the statistics show; it also reports industry-linked criticism of the evidence. The chapters that review the evidence disease by disease (chapters 2 to 10 of the 2006 report), where any dose-response or low-exposure data would sit, were not read. Certainty: very low. Status: single study.
population: Children and adults who do not smoke and are exposed to other people's tobacco smoke (secondhand smoke), as reviewed in the US Surgeon General's reports of 2006 (evidence to about 2005) and 2014
exposure: Breathing other people's tobacco smoke (secondhand smoke), at home, at work and elsewhere
comparator: People not exposed, or less exposed, to secondhand smoke, as defined in the studies the reports review (not read here)
outcome: Death and disease in children and in adults who do not smoke: sudden infant death, respiratory illness, ear disease, asthma, lung function, birth weight, lung cancer, coronary heart disease and stroke; and whether any level of exposure is without risk
magnitude: 2006 report, as summarized in its chapter 1: pooled studies indicate a 20 to 30 percent increase in the risk of lung cancer from secondhand smoke exposure associated with living with a person who smokes, and a 25 to 30 percent increase in the risk of coronary heart disease; 2014 report: an increase of about 20 to 30% in the risk of stroke. No relative risks, intervals or absolute risks are given in the part read for the children's outcomes or for the other adult outcomes; the size of the fall in coronary events after smokefree laws is not given in the conclusions. Grades by outcome as in the statement (sufficient, suggestive but not sufficient, inadequate). The 'no risk-free level' statement has no figure or threshold in the part read.

evidence.extracted: Secondhand smoke causes premature death and disease in children and in adults who do not smoke (1); children exposed are at increased risk of sudden infant death syndrome, acute respiratory infections, ear problems and more severe asthma, and smoking by parents causes respiratory symptoms and slows lung growth (2); in adults it has immediate adverse effects on the cardiovascular system and causes coronary heart disease and lung cancer (3).

evidence.locator: Chapter 1 › Chapter Conclusions › Chapter 2, conclusions 1 to 9
evidence.extracted: Conclusions bearing on a lowest safe level (the editors' reading; the report does not link them to the statement): more than 50 carcinogens in sidestream and secondhand smoke (1); sufficient that secondhand smoke and its condensates cause tumours in laboratory animals (2); sufficient that exposure of people who do not smoke raises urinary levels of metabolites of a tobacco-specific lung carcinogen (3); the mechanisms of lung cancer are probably similar to those in people who smoke, with the overall risk compared with active smoking diminished by a substantially lower carcinogenic dose (4); multiple mechanisms of respiratory tract injury (5) and mechanisms by which secondhand smoke could raise the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (6); sufficient: a clot-promoting effect (7), dysfunction of the cells lining blood vessels (8) and atherosclerosis in animal models (9).

evidence.locator: Chapter 1 › Chapter Conclusions › Chapter 5, conclusions 1 to 17
evidence.extracted: Reproductive and developmental effects, graded by the 2006 report. Sufficient to infer a causal relationship: sudden infant death syndrome (4) and a small reduction in birth weight from maternal exposure in pregnancy (6). Suggestive but not sufficient: preterm delivery (5) and childhood cancer overall with exposure before and after birth (11), leukaemias (14), lymphomas (15) and brain tumours (16). Inadequate to infer the presence or absence of a causal relationship: female fertility (1), spontaneous abortion (2), neonatal mortality (3), congenital malformations (7), cognitive functioning (8), behavioural problems (9), height and growth (10), childhood cancer from exposure in pregnancy alone (12) or in infancy alone (13), and other childhood cancers (17). Chapter 1 gives no relative risks for these.
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML, Surgeon General 2006 (rptsmokeexp): chapter 1 in full; chapters 2 to 10 not read

evidence.locator: Chapter 1 › Chapter Conclusions › Chapter 6, conclusions 1 to 12
evidence.extracted: Respiratory effects in children. Sufficient: lower respiratory illnesses in infants and children (1), with the greatest increase in risk from the mother's smoking (2); middle ear disease (3); cough, phlegm, wheeze and breathlessness (6) and ever having asthma (7) at school age; onset of wheeze illnesses in early childhood (8); persistent adverse effects on lung function across childhood from the mother's smoking in pregnancy (11); lower lung function in childhood from exposure after birth (12). Suggestive but not sufficient: natural history of middle ear effusion (4) and onset of childhood asthma (9). Inadequate: adenoidectomy or tonsillectomy (5) and allergy (10).

evidence.locator: Chapter 1 › Chapter Conclusions › Chapter 7, conclusions 1 to 6
evidence.extracted: Cancer in adults. Sufficient: lung cancer among people who never smoked, extending to all secondhand smoke exposure regardless of location (1); the pooled evidence indicates a 20 to 30 percent increase in the risk of lung cancer from secondhand smoke exposure associated with living with a person who smokes (2). Suggestive but not sufficient: breast cancer (3) and nasal sinus cancer (4). Inadequate: nasopharyngeal carcinoma (5) and cervical cancer (6).

evidence.extracted: Heart and blood vessels. Sufficient: coronary heart disease morbidity and mortality in men and women (1), with pooled relative risks from meta-analyses indicating a 25 to 30 percent increase in risk (2). Suggestive but not sufficient: stroke (3), and studies of subclinical vascular disease, particularly thickening of the carotid artery wall (4).

evidence.locator: Chapter 1 › Chapter Conclusions › Chapter 9, conclusions 1 to 14
evidence.extracted: Respiratory effects in adults. Sufficient: odour annoyance (1) and nasal irritation (2). Suggestive but not sufficient: acute respiratory symptoms in people with asthma (4) and in healthy people (5), chronic respiratory symptoms (6), short-term decline in lung function in people with asthma (7), a small decrement in lung function from chronic exposure (9), adult-onset asthma (11), worsening of asthma control (12) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (13). Inadequate: short-term lung function decline in healthy people (8), accelerated decline in lung function (10) and morbidity in people with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (14).

evidence.locator: Chapter 1 › Methodologic Issues › Misclassification of Secondhand Smoke Exposure, 3rd to 6th paragraphs; Misclassification of Secondhand Smoke Exposure › Use of Meta-Analysis, 3rd to 6th paragraphs; Confounding, 1st to 4th paragraphs (figure captions not counted)
evidence.extracted: Random misclassification of exposure tends to reduce the apparent effect; classifying some people who currently or formerly smoked as people who never smoked would push the lung cancer association upward when smoking clusters between spouses, but the analyses cited cannot fully explain the observed increase this way; because exposure has been widespread there are almost no truly unexposed people, so estimates may be biased downward. Meta-analysis is used with the recognition that the uncertainty around pooled estimates may exceed what conventional statistics show, because of biases in or selection of the studies; one analysis of 37 studies suggested that smaller studies gave higher risks, another found little evidence of publication bias, and efforts to find possibly missing studies are said to have yielded little or nothing that would alter published conclusions (the printed sentence is garbled); the pooled results were not decisive for the causal conclusions. Confounding: adults with more exposure tend to have less healthful lifestyles in US and UK surveys (how far this generalizes is uncertain), socioeconomic status may lie on the causal pathway, and confounding matters more as associations get weaker.
evidence.source_read: NCBI Bookshelf HTML, Surgeon General 2006 (rptsmokeexp): chapter 1 in full; chapters 2 to 10 not read

evidence.extracted: Process and grading: 22 experts wrote initial chapters, consolidated into 10, reviewed by more than 40 peer reviewers and more than 30 scientists for scientific integrity, then by agencies of the US Department of Health and Human Services; the same four levels as in the 2014 report, with consistency, strength, specificity (set aside as not relevant), temporality and coherence used as guidelines and not as a checklist; a small elevation of risk does not weigh against causality but alternative explanations need full exploration, and the risk is anticipated to be only slightly or modestly raised for some outcomes; reviews cover evidence identified through search strategies set out in each chapter (not read), mechanisms evidence was selectively reviewed, and newer key references are listed in an appendix.

risk_of_bias.note: Narrative reviews. Only the 2006 summary chapter was read; chapters 2 to 10, where the searches, pooled analyses and bias assessments are said to sit, were not, and no appraisal tool is named. The 2014 report states no search method.

inconsistency.note: Not rated: the reports grade each outcome separately and the 2014 report moves stroke from suggestive to sufficient with more evidence.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: no primary study was read. The statement that no exposure level is without risk is not backed by a threshold or dose-response analysis in the part read; the toxicology and mechanism conclusions are indirect evidence for it.

imprecision.note: No estimate is claimed beyond the pooled percentages the reports state.

publication_bias.note: The 2006 report discusses it (one analysis suggesting a small-study effect, another finding little) and reports that efforts to find missing studies yielded little or nothing that would alter its conclusions (the printed sentence is garbled); not rated further.

grade.reasoning: Findings of observational studies, biomarker and animal studies seen only through two narrative reviews. They start low (METHODS 6.3) and a claim seen only through reviews is downgraded for risk of bias (not appraisable) and indirectness (second-hand; the no-risk-free-level statement is supported only indirectly): very low, the floor. Very low here reflects how the claim is seen, not weak judgments by the reports, which grade many outcomes sufficient to infer a causal relationship. The relation is worded as an association; the causal wording belongs to the reports' own grades, which the statement attributes to them. Status single study: the 2014 report's secondhand smoke conclusions build on the 2006 report, so the two do not count as independent replication. The editors' reading of what the statement on a risk-free level rests on is labelled as theirs. It stays draft because it rests only on narrative reviews (METHODS 6.3 and 12). The 2006 report covers evidence to about 2005; the 2014 report updates stroke and adds smokefree law findings.

verification.flag_note: Draft for section 7 by the co-editor (decision p-ways-of-taking): held off the site until the senior author approves this version. Rests only on two Surgeon General's reports (narrative reviews): the 2006 chapter 1, read in full, and the 2014 chapter 1 conclusions. Chapters 2 to 10 of the 2006 report, where the searches, pooled analyses and any dose-response or low-exposure data sit, were not read, so what the statement on a risk-free level rests on is the editors' reading of which chapter 1 conclusions bear on it; reading chapters 2 (toxicology) and 8 (cardiovascular) would test that reading. Figure 1.1 of the 2014 report (conditions linked to secondhand smoke) is an image and was not read. No children's relative risks are in chapter 1.
